subChunks.title: Advanced Container Queries
subChunks.hookHtml: The Junior tier introduced container queries as a replacement for viewport breakpoints in components. This lesson goes deeper: named containers, container query units (cqw, cqh), container style queries, and the architectural patterns that make container queries the foundation of a truly reusable component library.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Maester Cordell: "A component that responds to its own container is a component that belongs in a library. A component that responds to the viewport is a component that belongs only in that specific layout. Container queries are the difference between a component and a utility."

Named containers — resolving nested container ambiguity

/* Without names, @sm: resolves to the nearest @container ancestor */
<div class="@container">
  <div class="@container">
    <div class="@sm:text-lg">
      /* Responds to inner container — is that what you want? */
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

/* With names, you target a specific ancestor */
<div class="@container/sidebar">
  <div class="@container/card">
    <div class="@sm/sidebar:text-lg">
      /* Explicitly responds to /sidebar, not /card */
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

Container query units: cqw and cqh

/* cqw = 1% of the container's width */
/* cqh = 1% of the container's height */
/* cqi = 1% of the container's inline size (usually width) */

<div class="@container">
  <!-- Text size based on container width, not viewport -->
  <h2 class="text-[3cqw] font-bold">
    Fluid heading scaled to container
  </h2>

  <!-- Image that fills exactly half the container width -->
  <img class="w-[50cqw]" />
</div>

The adaptive component pattern

/* A ProductCard that works in all contexts */
<div class="@container/product">
  <article class="
    flex flex-col
    @sm/product:flex-row
    @lg/product:grid @lg/product:grid-cols-[1fr_2fr]
    gap-4 bg-white rounded-xl border border-gray-100 overflow-hidden
  ">
    <!-- Thumbnail: full width → sidebar → fixed panel -->
    <div class="
      aspect-video
      @sm/product:aspect-square @sm/product:w-32 @sm/product:flex-none
      @lg/product:aspect-auto @lg/product:w-auto
      overflow-hidden
    ">
      <img class="w-full h-full object-cover" />
    </div>

    <div class="flex-1 p-4">
      <h3 class="font-semibold text-gray-900">Product Name</h3>
      <!-- Show description only at medium+ container -->
      <p class="hidden @md/product:block text-sm text-gray-500 mt-1">
        Description shown when container is at least md (448px)
      </p>
      <!-- Show extra metadata at large+ container -->
      <div class="hidden @lg/product:flex items-center gap-3 mt-3">
        <span class="text-sm font-medium text-blue-600">500 XP</span>
      </div>
    </div>
  </article>
</div>

Container style queries (CSS-native, limited support)

/* Style queries respond to computed style values on the container */
/* Browser support: Chrome 111+, limited — use @container (width) for now */

@container style(--featured: 1) {
  .card-title { font-size: 1.25rem; font-weight: 700; }
}

<div class="@container" style="--featured: 1">
  <h3 class="card-title">Featured card — larger title</h3>
</div>

Container queries vs media queries decision matrix

Use MEDIA QUERIES when:                 Use CONTAINER QUERIES when:
─ Page-level layout structure          ─ Component internal layout
─ Navigation visibility (mobile menu)  ─ Card grid item layout
─ Font size baseline                   ─ List item layout
─ Body/html level                      ─ Sidebar widget layout
─ Feature detection                    ─ Reusable library components

Maester Cordell: "The rule: if the component will ever appear in more than one layout context, use container queries. If you are making a page-level decision, use media queries. Most component decisions are container queries."

storyBeats.speaker: Maester Cordell
storyBeats.text: Named containers disambiguate nested @container contexts. Container query units (cqw, cqh) size elements relative to their container, not the viewport. Together these make components that are genuinely portable — drop them anywhere and they adapt correctly.

storyBeats.speaker: Named container targeting
storyBeats.text: Responds to outer, not inner

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build an adaptive quest card that uses a named container and shows three layout states:

  • .adv-container: @container/quest
  • .adv-card: flex, flex-col, @md/quest:flex-row, bg-white, rounded-xl, border, border-gray-100, overflow-hidden
  • .adv-image: aspect-video, @md/quest:aspect-square, @md/quest:w-36, @md/quest:flex-none, overflow-hidden
  • .adv-img: w-full, h-full, object-cover
  • .adv-body: flex-1, p-4
  • .adv-xp: hidden, @lg/quest:flex, items-center, gap-2, mt-2
  • .adv-desc: hidden, @md/quest:block, text-sm, text-gray-500, mt-1

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a three-panel layout where the same Article component adapts through 3 states based on its container: narrow (stacked image + title only), medium (side-by-side + description), wide (full layout with image, title, description, metadata, and CTA). Place the same component in containers of 280px, 480px, and 700px to verify. No starter code.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain when you would use a named container (@container/name) vs an unnamed @container. Give a concrete example where the unnamed container would produce the wrong result and the named container fixes it. What are container query units (cqw) and when would you use them?

questions.prompt: What does @container/card mean, and when do you need it instead of @container?
options: It names the container 'card' so children can target it specifically with @sm/card: — needed when multiple nested @container elements exist and you must target a specific ancestor
It applies container query behaviour only to elements with class 'card'
It's the v4 syntax for @container — the name is mandatory in v4
It creates a named CSS container-type: style that can be queried with @container style()
questions.answer: It names the container 'card' so children can target it specifically with @sm/card: — needed when multiple nested @container elements exist and you must target a specific ancestor
questions.explanation: Without a name, @sm: (and other container query variants) resolve to the nearest @container ancestor. When containers are nested, this may not be the container you want to query. Naming a container (@container/card) lets children use @sm/card: to explicitly target that container regardless of nesting depth.

questions.prompt: A heading uses class="text-[3cqw] font-bold" inside an @container. At 400px container width, what is the approximate font size?
options: 3px — cqw is 1/100th of a CSS pixel
3vw — cqw falls back to vw when inside a container
questions.explanation: 1cqw = 1% of the container's width. At 400px container width, 3cqw = 3% × 400px = 12px. This creates fluid typography that scales with the container rather than the viewport — useful for headings in adaptive components where the container width varies significantly across contexts.

questions.prompt: A navigation bar should collapse to a hamburger menu on mobile screens (viewport < 768px) regardless of which layout it appears in. A product card should stack vertically in a 300px sidebar but be horizontal in a 600px main column. Which breakpoint type should each use?
options: Navigation: media query (md:hidden) — viewport decision. Product card: container query (@md:flex-row) — container decision
Both should use container queries — container queries are always more accurate
Navigation: container query (the nav container is full-width, so it's the same as viewport). Product card: media query
Both should use media queries — container queries have limited browser support
questions.answer: Navigation: media query (md:hidden) — viewport decision. Product card: container query (@md:flex-row) — container decision
questions.explanation: Navigation collapse is a viewport-level decision — the nav always spans the full width, so viewport and container width are equivalent, and the intent is 'mobile device = collapsed'. Product card layout is a container decision — the same card appears in different-width columns on the same screen. Container queries ensure the card adapts to its actual space, not the screen size.
